title: Orphaned twice
hook: By eight, he had lost his father, his mother and his grandfather.

screens.text: **By the time he was eight,** he had lost his father, his mother and his grandfather. This episode is about grief, and about the people Allah kept sending.
**A trip with his mother.** At about six, he travelled with his mother, Aminah, to visit relatives in Madinah. On the way home, at a place called al-Abwa', she died [IslamQA 11575; Qalam ep. 14].
bubbles: According to the early biographers, Umm Ayman, a woman who helped care for him, brought the little boy home to Makkah [Qalam ep. 14].

cards.back: An Abyssinian woman in his family's household who cared for him from childhood. He later freed her [Qalam ep. 11].
Took the boy in and loved him dearly. He died when the boy was about eight [IslamQA 20240; Qalam ep. 15].
One more person was waiting to take him in. Keep going.

screens.text: **An uncle who stayed.** After his grandfather died, his uncle Abu Talib took him in. Abu Talib didn't have much money, but he loved his nephew like his own children, and he would protect him for more than forty years [IslamQA 20240; IslamQA 11575].
Each time he lost someone, someone else was there.

events.title: His father dies
events.text: 'Abdullah dies before his son is born [IslamQA 11575].

events.title: His mother dies
events.text: Aminah dies at al-Abwa' on the way home from Madinah. Umm Ayman brings him home, the early biographers say [Qalam ep. 14].

events.title: His grandfather's home
events.text: 'Abd al-Muttalib takes him in and loves him dearly [IslamQA 20240].

events.title: His grandfather dies
events.text: Another loss, before he is even nine [IslamQA 20240; Qalam ep. 15].

events.title: Abu Talib
events.text: His uncle raises him and protects him for over forty years [IslamQA 11575].

screens.text: **Years later, a reminder.** When he was a grown man and a prophet, the Qur'an looked back on this childhood: *"Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] refuge?"* [Q 93:6, Saheeh Intl.]
bubbles: The **surah** goes on: *"And He found you lost and guided [you], And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient"* [Q 93:7–8, Saheeh Intl.].

options.feedback: Yes. Allah reminded him that every loss had been met with shelter.
Not quite. The verse says orphan: a boy who lost his parents and was still given refuge.
Not quite. It looks back on his childhood: Allah found him an orphan and sheltered him.

screens.text: **Allah sends people.** Each time he lost someone, someone else stepped in: Umm Ayman on the road, his grandfather, then his uncle. If becoming Muslim has cost you closeness with your family, you aren't forgotten.
bubbles: Sometimes the people He sends are a mentor, a friend from the masjid, a neighbour. Sometimes they come slowly. Keep your door open.

screens.situation: Luis's mom stopped calling after he became Muslim. His grandma still has him over for Sunday lunch, and a brother from the masjid texts him before Friday prayer. Luis feels like he's lost his family.

options.text: Let himself grieve, keep a kind door open with his mom, and lean on the people who are there
options.feedback: Yes. The grief is real, the door stays open, and the people Allah sent are worth leaning on.

options.text: Cut his mom off, since she cut him off
options.feedback: Not quite. Islam asks him to keep treating his parents well, even when it's hard [Q 31:14–15].

options.text: Pretend it doesn't hurt; real faith means not feeling sad
options.feedback: Not quite. The Prophet ﷺ wept when his little son died [Bukhari 1303]. Sadness isn't weak faith.

screens.text: He lost almost everyone, and Allah never once left him without someone who loved him.
Next episode: a shepherd, a trader, and a pact to stand up for the wronged.

check.prompt: Who raised the Prophet ﷺ after his grandfather died?

options.feedback: Right. Poor, but loving, and he protected him for over forty years.
Not quite. Halimah nursed him as a baby. After his grandfather died, his uncle Abu Talib raised him.

check.prompt: What does Q 93:6 remind him of?

options.text: Allah found him an orphan and gave him refuge
options.feedback: Right. Every loss in his childhood was met with shelter from Allah.

options.text: He should have been an orphan forever
options.feedback: Not quite. The verse is about Allah sheltering him: He found him an orphan and gave him refuge.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- At about six he travelled with his mother Aminah to visit relatives in Madinah; on the way back she died at al-Abwa' [IslamQA 11575; Qalam ep. 14].
- Umm Ayman (Barakah) brought him home, according to the early biographers [Qalam ep. 14] (reports differ on whether she went to Madinah first).
- Umm Ayman was an Abyssinian woman in his family's household; he inherited her and later freed her (the early biographers say at his marriage to Khadijah) [Qalam ep. 11]. (scholar question Q40)
- His grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib took him in, loved him dearly, and died when the boy was about eight [IslamQA 20240; IslamQA 11575; Qalam ep. 15].
- His uncle Abu Talib, his father's full brother, then raised him; poor, loving, and protective for over forty years [IslamQA 20240; IslamQA 11575].
- The Qur'an: "Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] refuge?" [Q 93:6–8].

**Likely questions**
- *"Where are his parents (or Abu Talib) in the afterlife?"* This is sensitive, especially for converts with non-Muslim parents. Answer gently and briefly: there are authentic hadith on this [Muslim 976; Bukhari 1360], and scholars discuss them in different ways. Don't deny the texts and don't speculate about any person. Stress that Allah alone judges, with perfect justice and mercy. Offer "Ask my imam" for the detail. (scholar question Q42)
- *"What about my own non-Muslim parents?"* Respond with care first. Point to Day 77 for grief and what's open to them now: keeping ties, kindness, du'a for their guidance while they're alive [Q 31:14–15]. Never comment on any individual's fate. For a parent who has died, follow Day 77's handling and offer the imam. (scholar question Q23)
- *"Was Umm Ayman a slave?"* Say plainly that slavery existed everywhere at that time, that she was in his family's household, and that he freed her. Don't claim slavery is acceptable today or that Islam abolished it in one stroke; detailed questions go to the imam. (scholar question Q40)
- *"How did Abu Talib protect him?"* Later episodes (12, 15, 16) cover how Abu Talib stood by him during persecution. Keep it to that now.
- *"My family pulled away; how do I cope?"* Listen first. Grief over distance is real; keep a kind door open [Q 31:14–15]; lean on the mentor and masjid. If there's danger at home, follow the safety rule.

**Escalate:** the afterlife of his parents or Abu Talib beyond the gentle outline above (Q42); a convert's own deceased non-Muslim relative (Q23); detailed questions on slavery (Q40); any unsafe family situation (safety rule, never only the imam queue).

**Don't**
- Don't raise the afterlife of his parents or Abu Talib unless asked, and never on a screen.
- Don't quote Muslim 976 or Bukhari 1360 word for word to someone grieving; summarise gently if asked.
- Don't speculate about anyone's fate in the hereafter.
- Don't use the convert's family situation to pressure them.
